title: Health tech grant contribution and 2026 parking rates
subtitle: Highway salt contract, demolition relief, a high-rise Uptown public meeting, and a homes association levy update.
overview: Council committed up to $540,000 from the Economic Development Reserve over three years to support the City's application to the Province's Trade-Impacted Communities Program, for a health tech accelerator tied to the new hospital {{vote:m6}}. It also approved 2026 parking rates, with a 3.5% increase to monthly permits and no change to hourly rates {{vote:m8}}, and awarded the highway salt contract {{vote:m7}}.

A consent motion approved a boundary road agreement with the Township of Woolwich, a new Compensation and Benefits Policy, and relief from demolition control requirements for two sets of residential properties. Council received an update on a Special Service Area Levy vote for the Upper Beechwood Homes Association as information {{vote:m9}}. Ballots are due September 29, and council is to decide on any resulting by-law on October 27.

In the evening, council held an informal public meeting on a proposed Uptown tower at 9-47 Erb Street West. No decision was made; staff will report back at a formal meeting. A Blue Box notice of motion was tabled for September 29. Council also met in closed session for training, with no decisions reported.

decisions.detail: Council approved the City's grant application and up to $540,000 from the Economic Development Reserve over three years, with signing authority if the application succeeds.
Council approved a 3.5% increase to monthly parking permits and no hourly rate increase for 2026, with 2027-2035 forecasts approved in principle and the fees by-law updated.
Council awarded RFQ25-33 for treated and coarse highway salt to Compass Minerals Canada Corp. for a total of $1,173,832.63 including unrecoverable HST.
Council authorized the Mayor and Clerk to sign the Boundary Road Maintenance and Improvement Agreement with the Township of Woolwich, subject to staff and solicitor satisfaction.
Council approved the Compensation and Benefits Policy attached to report CORP2025-029.

decisions.item: Demolitions at King and Caroline Streets South
decisions.detail: Council granted relief from demolition control by-law requirements for 215 King Street South and 176, 180 and 182 Caroline Street South, including a six-year construction start deadline.

decisions.item: Demolitions at Erb Street West and Dunbar Road North
decisions.detail: Council granted similar relief for six Erb Street West properties and 5 Dunbar Road North, with a five-year deadline to start construction.

debate: On the health tech grant, one councillor asked how the accelerator would relate to existing hospital-linked innovation programs; the Accelerator Centre said the aim is to complement, not duplicate. Others asked how private investment would be tracked and whether hardware, not just software, would be supported. Staff said the program leans toward software to balance the region's device focus.

On parking, a councillor asked why some permit lots were discontinued. Staff said an overnight lot was too small to plow practically, one lot had been renamed, and a recreation centre lot no longer had a business needing permits or spare daytime capacity.

At the Erb Street West public meeting, residents raised concerns about archaeological potential, shadows on a nearby park and homes, reflections, traffic, building heat and ventilation, elevators and fire department capacity. One delegate also called for fewer parking floors and more family-sized units. Several councillors asked staff to consider a Phase One archaeological study.

Other residents spoke in support, citing the housing shortage, the nearby light rail station, and the need for more activity around the Public Square. Councillors asked about the amount of parking, lost commercial space, accessible ramps, mural planning, energy efficiency and flood-related design. They also raised third-party peer review of studies and whether a tower this tall is appropriate given stalled approved projects.

Staff said the site sits in a special policy area for flood hazards, so the province must approve any change. They said the technical studies are still under review, and that the 120-day review period can run longer on complex applications when applicants must update studies.
